it's awesome to see the reception here 🔥 

one of the jev's promises is to make a lot of business operations extremely lightweight and fast, while still saving intelligence-heavy tasks for larger agentic systems

docjev is hyperfocused on doc classification and splitting, and it's very good at it. you can see the full visual report from the readme: https://t.co/PH4A43TN89

quotedTweet.text:
Introducing DocJev - a lightning-fast OSS library for document classification and splitting with jev ⚡️

Give a document alongside some natural language category rules. Jev will predict the document category (classify) or the boundaries between sub-documents (split).

It is 6x faster than gpt-5.6-luna with equivalent accuracy.

You can choose between different OCR backends:
liteparse: the fastest/most accurate free+OSS text parser out there. Perfect for digitalized documents. The speedups vs. luna above are inclusive of liteparse times.
LlamaParse: the most advanced VLM-based solution for complex docs. Using this will of course add latency on document preprocessing. But it’s a good option if you want to cache the digitalized representations of documents for a variety of downstream tasks.

Check it out: https://t.co/PVE4hbEyFR

If you want to dive deeper into liteparse or LlamaParse check the links below:
liteparse: https://t.co/JNER0mVcB8
LlamaParse: https://t.co/XYZmx5TFz8
quotedTweet.translationZh:
推出 DocJev：一个用于文档分类和拆分的超高速 OSS 库，基于 jev ⚡️

只需提供一份文档和一些自然语言类别规则。Jev 会预测文档类别（分类），或预测子文档之间的边界（拆分）。

在准确率相当的情况下，它比 gpt-5.6-luna 快 6 倍。

你可以选择不同的 OCR 后端：
liteparse：目前最快、最准确的免费 + OSS 文本解析器。非常适合数字化文档。上述相较 luna 的提速已包含 liteparse 的耗时。
LlamaParse：最先进的基于 VLM 的复杂文档解决方案。使用它当然会增加文档预处理延迟。但如果你想缓存文档的数字化表示，用于各种下游任务，这是一个不错的选择。

posts.text:
LangChain 这篇「Jev-as-a-Judge」是关于 Jev 的很好的实践。

每次 Agent 改完一版，分数涨了，我们不知道到底是它变强了，还是裁判这次手松了？

LangChain 在文章里讲它测了一个很实际的问题：让 Jev 给 Agent 打分，能不能更快、更便宜，也更稳定。

做法很直接，把 Agent 的回答和工具调用等信息交给 Jev，让它按标准返回分数或通过／不通过。它直接输出判断和概率，省去了逐字生成评语的过程。

实验中，Jev 平均每次评估耗时 0.44 秒，成本约 0.00035 美元。更值得注意的是，同一份回答反复打分，它的评分方差只有几款对照模型的 1/92～1/913。

不过，这里只有 5 条固定的天气任务记录，每条重复评估 100 次。它说明了这组测试里的稳定性，还不足以证明 Jev 在复杂任务上普遍判得更准。裁判也可能一直稳定地判错。

我更看好它对 Agent 迭代的意义。评估足够快、足够便宜，就有机会覆盖更多真实运行记录，更早发现改动带来的退步。

前提是先把裁判校准好。尤其要用这些分数驱动 Agent 自我改进时，反馈越密，判断偏差也越容易被反复强化。

quotedTweet.text:
TypeSafe AI's Jev kept coming up, so I decided to test it on a task using public medical literature.
Jev lets you describe a decision in natural language and get structured answers with probabilities. I used it to identify sentences reporting suspected adverse drug effects.
It found most relevant sentences, but also flagged many negatives and sometimes gave incorrect answers complete confidence.
I then connected Jev to GEPA, a prompt optimizer, to see whether clearer instructions would help. An assistant proposed revisions based on training errors, and GEPA evaluated the candidates.
The selected prompt clarified the evidence needed in each sentence: a drug, a harmful effect, and a relationship between them.
On the same 300 fresh test sentences:
✅ F1 increased from 69.1% to 79.7%.
✅ False positives fell from 47 to 22.
✅ Probability error, measured by Brier score, fell by about 45%.

🔗https://t.co/f5irITgYDU

posts.text:
Skill 越装越多，Agent 可能先被自己的「说明书」塞满 Context。

Cornell 和 Microsoft Research Cambridge 这篇论文，对比了两种很常见的 Skill 用法：

一种是调用 Skill 后，把 SKILL.md 直接塞进主 Agent 的上下文里；

另一种是把 Skill 交给独立 Subagent，让它在自己的 Context 里完成任务，最后只把结果返回主 Agent。

差别看起来不大，但长任务里会被迅速放大。

主 Agent 一旦同时背着 Skill 指令、工具输出和历史轨迹，Context 很容易越来越重。Subagent 则能把一部分执行过程隔离出去。

论文发现，当 Skill 本身写得足够清楚，明确输入、步骤和输出时，交给 Subagent 效果更好。

以 GPT-5.3 Codex 为例，95.3% 的任务都降低了峰值 Context 长度。

代价是 Context 更干净了，但 Agent 之间来回传递信息，会增加总 Token。

我觉得可以把 Skill 理解成一种「接口」。

简单知识可以直接放进 Context，复杂流程更适合封装起来独立执行。

Skill 越装越多，Agent 可能先被自己的「说明书」塞满 Context。

Cornell 和 Microsoft Research Cambridge 这篇论文，对比了两种很常见的 Skill 用法：

一种是调用 Skill 后，把 SKILL.md 直接塞进主 Agent 的上下文里；

另一种是把 Skill 交给独立 Subagent，让它在自己的 Context 里完成任务，最后只把结果返回主 Agent。

差别看起来不大，但长任务里会被迅速放大。

主 Agent 一旦同时背着 Skill 指令、工具输出和历史轨迹，Context 很容易越来越重。Subagent 则能把一部分执行过程隔离出去。

论文发现，当 Skill 本身写得足够清楚，明确输入、步骤和输出时，交给 Subagent 效果更好。

以 GPT-5.3 Codex 为例，95.3% 的任务都降低了峰值 Context 长度。

代价是 Context 更干净了，但 Agent 之间来回传递信息，会增加总 Token。

我觉得可以把 Skill 理解成一种「接口」。

简单知识可以直接放进 Context，复杂流程更适合封装起来独立执行。

📎 arxiv: https://t.co/NKpLXGEifz

很推荐 Thorsten Ball 这篇关于「软件开发未来」的判断。

里面不少观点都很激进，我也不一定全部认同，但确实把 AI Coding 再往前推几年之后可能发生的变化想得很彻底。

英文内容比较多，我按原意压缩成中文：

• Code Review 会消失，单元测试也可能消失。人不会再逐行检查模型生成的代码，而是更多去 Review 整个系统。

• 「写代码」这门手艺会慢慢弱化，但「做软件」会更重要。真正值钱的是知道该解决什么问题、什么时候发布、怎么获得反馈。

• 大多数 Bug 可能会变成「你让 AI 做错了东西」，而不是代码本身写错了。

• Terminal、编辑器、CLI 这些工具也可能被 Agent 吞掉。人不需要再记命令和参数，只需要表达自己想做什么。

• PM、Design、Engineering 的传统分工会被重新打散。只负责传 Ticket、协调流程的人，价值可能会快速下降。

• 「好代码」的定义也会变。很多规范本来就是为了方便人类阅读和维护，如果未来大部分代码都由机器修改，这些标准未必还那么重要。

• Token 甚至可能成为新的生产力门槛。谁能调用更强的模型、拥有更多推理资源，谁的软件生产能力就可能更强。

• UI 也可能开始按需生成。很多菜单、设置页、Dashboard，本质上都是人在适应不会理解自然语言的软件。如果软件真的能理解意图，很多固定 UI 可能都不再需要。

我比较有感触的一点是：

软件开发的中心，可能会慢慢从「怎么把代码写出来」，转向「到底该让机器做什么，以及怎么判断它做对了」。

Code Review、单测、Terminal 会不会真的「死」，这些都可以争。

但如果 AI Coding 继续这样发展，很多今天看起来理所当然的软件工程习惯，可能都值得重新问一遍：

「为什么还需要它？」

LangChain 这篇「Jev-as-a-Judge」是关于 Jev 的很好的实践。

每次 Agent 改完一版，分数涨了，我们不知道到底是它变强了，还是裁判这次手松了？

LangChain 在文章里讲它测了一个很实际的问题：让 Jev 给 Agent 打分，能不能更快、更便宜，也更稳定。

做法很直接，把 Agent 的回答和工具调用等信息交给 Jev，让它按标准返回分数或通过／不通过。它直接输出判断和概率，省去了逐字生成评语的过程。

实验中，Jev 平均每次评估耗时 0.44 秒，成本约 0.00035 美元。更值得注意的是，同一份回答反复打分，它的评分方差只有几款对照模型的 1/92～1/913。

不过，这里只有 5 条固定的天气任务记录，每条重复评估 100 次。它说明了这组测试里的稳定性，还不足以证明 Jev 在复杂任务上普遍判得更准。裁判也可能一直稳定地判错。

我更看好它对 Agent 迭代的意义。评估足够快、足够便宜，就有机会覆盖更多真实运行记录，更早发现改动带来的退步。

前提是先把裁判校准好。尤其要用这些分数驱动 Agent 自我改进时，反馈越密，判断偏差也越容易被反复强化。

reviewedPosts.author: c_valenzuelab
reviewedPosts.text:
I read about an experiment where people are paid to build little Lego action figures called Bionicles. They’re paid for each one they complete, but each one pays a little less than the last. $2 for finishing the first one, $1.89 for the second, and 11 cents less for each one after.

The builders are split into two groups. In one group, each Lego figure is taken apart after it’s finished and the pieces put back in the box. In the other, completed figures are kept intact and lined up on the desk in front of them. The more figures they build, the fuller the desk gets.

The second group keeps building longer, even as they get paid less and less.

People want to get paid, sure, but they also want their work to amount to something. At the most basic level, they want their work not to disappear the second it’s done. And that’s just in an experiment.

In real life, work gets tangled up with who you are and how you spend your life. People want something to show for their work. They want to see their creations in their hands, on screen, on display, out in the real world. They want to go to dinner with friends and family, show them something, and say, I made that.

The Valley likes its binaries. Mercenaries versus missionaries. And all the talk about how much we prefer to work with the latter. The Lego experiment draws out a third motivation that the binary misses. For makers, making the thing and the finished thing itself are part of the reward, along with the simple recognition of having made it.

The headlines make AI research look a lot like free agency. Researchers swapping team jerseys and getting poached by big labs and bigger offers. Some of this is real. But the best people always have options. A lot of companies can pay them well. Not that many can give them something genuinely hard and new to work on that really matters.

There are different kinds of things people want to have made.

Some people want to take a new capability and figure out how to package it, get it into people’s hands, make it a bit more useful. Others want to be on the ground floor of creating an entirely new capability. Every technology wave has people moving the frontier, and others figuring out what to build with what just became possible.

I’ve always been drawn to creating that new thing. There’ll always be another chance to arbitrage what’s already been made. And there’s something hard to really price about getting to create the primitive that other people eventually build on. That motivation to keep finding the next crazy thing has kept me playing the long game.

The beauty of building on the frontier is there’s reward on both ends.

There’s a reward while you’re making the thing, especially when it’s hard enough that you don’t know if you can and important enough that people care that you figure it out. Then there’s the thing you’ve brought to life. Over time, the artifacts add up to a body of work. And the body of work becomes part of the reward.

The long-term version of this is pretty simple. Once people make one thing they’re proud of, they tend to want to make another. And it’s nice when the people you spend all day making stuff with feel like your kind of people, and you admire them. You admire how they think, how they approach their craft, their values and standards, their taste.

An underappreciated part of choosing where you work is choosing who you want to become more like.

The pay should still be good. Great, even. But by then, it’s not the only thing keeping you there. A place where you keep getting to make things you’re proud of, surrounded by people you respect, becomes a place you want to stay.

Mercenaries want money. Missionaries want purpose. Makers want to make. They may want money and purpose too, but they want them by way of what they create. Makers want something they’re proud to have made, with people they’re proud to have made it with. Something they hope stays standing when the work is done.

Something to show for it.
